name: Riemann Curvature
kick: gravity & geometry · differential geometry · order matters when space curves
title: Curvature as the failure of moves to commute — why 90 degrees on a globe, 0 on a flat sheet
lede: On a flat piece of paper, the order of your moves does not matter: go east then north lands you in the same spot as go north then east. But on a curved surface like a globe, the order matters. Take a small loop on Earth and see if your arrow comes back pointing the same way — it does not. That rotation is curvature. Curvature is exactly the fact that operations fail to commute. Here is how to measure it, why it shows up on a globe but not a flat sheet, and why the same 'order matters' idea runs both gravity and quantum mechanics.
arc: Why the round trip rotates the arrow

sections.h2: 1 · The problem — does the order of two moves ever matter?

blocks.html: Consider yourself on a flat sheet of paper. Start at a point, go 1 meter east, then 1 meter north — you end up at a corner. Now rewind and try it the other way: go 1 meter north, then 1 meter east. You end up in the same corner. The order of your moves did not change your destination. In the language of mathematics, these two moves commute — you get the same result no matter which order you do them in.

But what if the surface you travel on is curved? The question: on a curved surface, does the order of two small moves still not matter, or does it matter now? The answer to this question is precisely what curvature measures.

sections.h2: 2 · The reframe — test curvature by seeing if things commute

blocks.html: To measure curvature from the inside, you do not need to step outside the surface and look at its shape. Instead, you carry a direction (an arrow) around a closed loop — a small triangle or square on the surface — without rotating it by your own hand. You just keep the arrow parallel to itself as you move along the edges. When you arrive back where you started, look at your arrow: does it point the same way as it did at the start, or has it rotated?

On a flat sheet, the arrow always comes back unchanged. The order of moves does not affect your arrow's orientation either. But on a curved surface, the arrow comes back rotated. How much it rotates depends on how much area is enclosed in your loop and how curved the surface is. This rotation — this failure of the arrow to return unchanged — is curvature. In other words, curvature is the discovery that the order of two moves is not commutative on a curved space.

The hidden quantity is the Riemann curvature — how much a vector rotates when carried around a tiny loop, which depends on the two directions framing the loop; it is curvature recorded direction by direction.

sections.h2: 3 · Seen on a real run — the 90-degree rotation on a globe

blocks.html: We carried an arrow around a triangle on a globe, always keeping it parallel to itself (parallel transport). The triangle: go a quarter turn west along the equator, then straight north to the North Pole, then straight south back to where you started. Never twist or rotate the arrow by hand; just keep moving with it.

blocks.caption: A quarter-turn along the equator equals one quarter of the sphere's circumference — an area equal to one eighth of the Earth's surface. The rotation of the arrow equals the enclosed area times the surface's curvature.

blocks.html: The discovered fact: carry an arrow around a quarter-octant triangle on Earth and it rotates exactly 90 degrees. On a flat sheet, the same triangle leaves the arrow unchanged (0 degrees). The rotation is a direct, from-the-inside measurement of curvature. You can compute the rotation in advance if you know the enclosed area and the curvature. The formula is simple: rotation = area times curvature. For one quarter of one eighth of a sphere, the rotation equals the sphere's total curvature, which is 1 in units of inverse area. A flat sheet has curvature 0, so the rotation is 0.

sections.h2: 4 · Why the round trip rotates the arrow — order fails to commute on a curve

blocks.html: Picture a smaller and smaller triangle on the surface. As it shrinks, the rotation of your arrow also shrinks. But the rotation per unit area stays roughly constant — that constant is the curvature at that spot. Now think of the triangle as made of two infinitesimal moves: a tiny step in the north direction, then a tiny step in the east direction, then back — south, west, back to the start. If you go north-then-east versus east-then-north, you retrace a different shape, and the extra rotation you pick up is curvature.

On a flat sheet, going north then east lands you at exactly the same spot as going east then north. The two paths enclose zero area, and your arrow picks up zero rotation. The two moves commute. But on a globe, because the surface is not flat, the two small steps in different orders carve out a tiny enclosed area. That area, though infinitesimal, has a definite curvature — and your arrow picks up a proportional rotation. The smaller the moves, the smaller the area, but the curvature (area-adjusted) is always the same at a given point. This is the meaning of curvature: it is the obstruction to commutativity, measured per unit area.

sections.h2: 5 · The one real limit — it is a local, infinitesimal quantity

blocks.html: The curvature at a single point is a single number, or at least can be thought of as a single number along any pair of directions. But on an entire surface or in higher-dimensional spaces, curvature becomes more complex. In three dimensions, space is not just curved or flat in one direction — it can bend differently along different axes. A sphere curves the same way in all directions (isotropic), but the surface of a cylinder curves in one direction (lengthwise) and not in another. In spacetime, which has 4 dimensions (three space, one time), there are many more independent curvatures to track.

Also, this test — carrying an arrow around a loop — only works well for infinitesimal loops. For large loops, the geometry becomes complicated. And the rotation depends entirely on the area enclosed, not on the shape of the loop itself. So if two different loops enclose the same area on the same curved surface, the arrow rotates the same amount for both. That is powerful — a single number per point characterizes curvature everywhere — but it also means you need the full arsenal of tensors and higher mathematics to write down all the curvatures in higher dimensions.

sections.h2: 6 · The surprise — curvature runs gravity, and the commutator runs quantum mechanics

blocks.html: This idea — that curvature is the failure of operations to commute — appears in Einstein's general relativity in a more elaborate form. In spacetime, curvature is how mass warps geometry, and every object in free fall follows a geodesic (the straightest available path) through that warped spacetime. The path curves not because a force pulls on it, but because the geometry itself is curved. The commutator-like object in spacetime is called the Riemann curvature tensor, a multi-component mathematical object that captures all the ways spacetime can warp. Einstein's equation says that this tensor is proportional to the matter and energy density — mass makes spacetime curve, and curved spacetime tells things how to move.

And there is a stunning echo in quantum mechanics. In quantum theory, the order of operations matters intensely. The commutator — the difference between doing operation A then operation B versus doing B then A — is one of the fundamental objects. It even appears in Heisenberg's uncertainty principle: position and momentum do not commute, and the commutator between them is a fixed tiny number (Planck's constant divided by 2π). So whether you are transporting an arrow on a curved surface, bending spacetime with mass, or manipulating quantum states, the same architecture applies: measure the failure of operations to commute, and you read off the structure of the system. Curvature, gravity, and quantum jumps all flow from this one principle.

sections.h2: 7 · Where it is used in practice — Curvature is where operations stop commuting

blocks.html: Inertial measurement units in spacecraft and submarines detect curvature by finding that moving forward-then-turn is not the same as turn-then-move-forward; the difference tells the platform's position and orientation in curved spacetime or in Earth's gravity field. Precision gyroscopes used in geodesy and navigation accumulate phase shifts as they process in curved spacetime; the cumulative shift reveals the strength of curvature. Quantum interference experiments send particles around loops in electromagnetic or gravitational potentials and measure phase shifts that depend on the enclosed area and the curvature of the field. Gravitational wave detectors (like LIGO) sense tidal curvature by comparing how nearby test masses are pushed differently—this differential motion is the signature that operations (displacements) do not commute in curved spacetime.

An inertial platform that turns north-then-east versus east-then-north will end up at slightly different headings because the Earth's curvature makes the two paths close different loops. The discrepancy is tiny on short paths but accumulates over long journeys and reveals both Earth's curvature and the platform's orientation. Gyroscope precession in curved spacetime happens because parallel transport of the spin vector around a closed loop returns it rotated; the rotation rate per unit area is the local Riemann curvature. Quantum phase accumulation (Berry phase, topological phases) comes from parallel transport of quantum states and is analogous to vector rotation—the phase depends on the enclosed area and the curvature of the quantum state space. In LIGO, two perpendicular test masses feel slightly different gravitational acceleration because they are at slightly different positions in curved spacetime; this tidal effect is a direct probe of curvature.
Non-commutativity is the signature of curvature in any context—classical mechanics, general relativity, or quantum mechanics—because curvature is the obstruction to perfect commutativity.

recipe.summary: Script: scripts/experiments/gr_run.py. Carry an arrow (a vector) around a closed triangle on a curved surface (a sphere), using parallel transport to keep it always parallel to itself (never rotating by hand). Measure the rotation angle when the arrow returns to the start. Compare a quarter-octant triangle (area = 1/8 sphere) on Earth versus the same triangle on a flat sheet. The rotation equals the enclosed area times the local curvature; on a sphere it is 90 degrees, on flat space it is 0 degrees.
recipe.eq:
rotation angle = enclosed area × curvature
for a sphere of radius R: curvature = 1/R^2
for Earth (R ≈ 6371 km): a quarter-octant (area ≈ 1/8 sphere) → rotation = 90 degrees
for flat sheet: curvature = 0 → rotation = 0 degrees
recipe.note: Full script: scripts/experiments/gr_run.py (EXP1). Numbers are the run's output verbatim. Parallel transport is the method; curvature-as-non-commuting is the interpretation.
